theme: Unit 14 review, The Return & the Chronicles Perspective
memoryText: Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse stands near the end of the Old Testament like a lamp in a dark room. After centuries of kings who failed, a king is promised who will not. Every phrase counts.

“Behold.” The word calls us to stop and look. Something is about to be shown.

“Your king is coming to you.” The king is not a distant ruler. He comes to his people. After the return, the Jews had no king of their own. They were governed by Persians. The promise is that their king would come in person. The one who comes belongs to them and comes toward them.

“Righteous.” Every earthly king in the Old Testament had flaws. Even David failed. This king is righteous, fully and perfectly. He does what is right.

“And having salvation is he.” The phrase can mean he is saved, or he brings salvation. Both are true. He is delivered by God and he delivers others. His mission is to save.

“Humble.” The Hebrew word means afflicted or lowly. This king comes not with power but in weakness. He enters Jerusalem not in the pride of a conqueror but in the humility of a servant.

“Mounted on a donkey.” The picture is of peace. The next verse says he will cut off the war horse and speak peace to the nations. The kingdom he brings does not come by the sword.

When Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, the crowds shouted, “Hosanna!” They were seeing this verse come true. He was the king who came to them, righteous, saving, and humble, and he would give his life.
unitRecap: Unit 14 closed the Old Testament with a partial return. You saw God keep his word through Cyrus, bringing a remnant home to rebuild the altar, the temple, and the wall. In Ezra and Nehemiah, you read of prayer and obstruction, of the word of God read aloud, and of joy and tears mingled, followed by the sad return to old sins. In Esther, you saw God’s hidden hand preserve his people in a foreign land. In Chronicles, the whole story was retold for the returned community, from Adam to Cyrus, with David’s covenant at its center and the repeated call to seek the LORD. Then the prophets of the return spoke. Joel called for hearts to be torn and promised the Spirit. Obadiah warned against pride and standing aloof. Haggai stirred the builders. Zechariah showed a clean Joshua, a humble king on a donkey, a pierced one, an opened fountain, and a Lord who will be king over all the earth. Malachi ended with love, a sharp rebuke, and a promise: a messenger, a Lord who will come suddenly to his temple, a sun of righteousness, and Elijah before the day. The Old Testament closes with its promises unfulfilled. The people are home, but the glory is not yet fully back, and the king has not come. Four hundred years of silence will follow, but the promise stands. Everything you have read from Genesis to Malachi has been preparing for the Gospel.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does the post-exilic community’s joy at the Temple’s rebuilding turn to weeping?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about Ezra 3:10-13 and Haggai 2:3. What did the old men remember, and what does the contrast say about the return being partial?

reviewQuestions.question: What does Chronicles add to our understanding of the monarchy?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Consider the Chronicler’s focus on David, the temple, and the repeated call to “seek the LORD.” How does it differ from Kings, and what does it say to a people with no king?

reviewQuestions.question: How does Malachi set up the 400 years of silence before Christ?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look at Malachi 3:1, 4:2, and 4:5-6. What promises are left hanging, and who do the Gospels say fulfills them?

reviewQuestions.question: What do the visions in Zechariah reveal about the coming Messiah?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think of the Branch, the priest on his throne, the humble king on a donkey, the shepherd sold for thirty pieces of silver, and the pierced one. How do these pictures fit together?

prayerPrompts: Thank God for carrying his people through exile and return.
Thank him for the promises that point to Christ.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
